title: Sorting descending and "sort ascending then reverse the list" give different answers when there are ties
assumption: sorted(data, reverse=True) is exactly the same as list(reversed(sorted(data))) — descending sort and "sort then flip the list" are interchangeable.

input.display: [("a",1), ("b",1), ("c",2)] sorted descending by the second element, two different ways
input.description: Showing the highest-scoring rows first, where some rows tie on score and the tiebreaker is "whoever was already first stays first" (e.g. insertion order, or an earlier sort by name).

what_goes_wrong: sorted(data, key=..., reverse=True) returns [("c",2), ("a",1), ("b",1)] — among the tied score-1 rows, "a" still comes before "b", matching their original order. list(reversed(sorted(data, key=...))) returns [("c",2), ("b",1), ("a",1)] — the SAME tied rows now come out with "b" before "a", the opposite of their original order. The non-tied row ("c",2) ends up in the same place either way; only the ties disagree.
why: A stable sort keeps elements that compare equal in their original relative order. Python documents reverse=True as sorting "as if each comparison were reversed" while staying stable, so tied rows keep their input order, and a JavaScript comparator that negates the ascending comparison does the same. Reversing an already-sorted list flips every position, including the order inside each group of ties. The two only agree when there are no ties.

repros.code:
data = [("a", 1), ("b", 1), ("c", 2)]
by_reverse_flag = sorted(data, key=lambda t: t[1], reverse=True)
by_sort_then_reverse = list(reversed(sorted(data, key=lambda t: t[1])))
print(by_reverse_flag)
print(by_sort_then_reverse)
print(by_reverse_flag == by_sort_then_reverse)

fix: If tie order matters for a descending sort, use the language's actual descending sort (reverse=True in Python, or a comparator that negates the ascending comparison in JS) rather than sorting ascending and reversing the whole list afterward — they are not equivalent whenever ties exist.
